title: The Truth Behind Cage-Free and Free-Range
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the difference between cage free and free range egg and poultry labels. They cover the history of battery cages after industrialization in the 1950s, the welfare problems of caged laying hens (no room to move, no privacy for laying, beak trimming, forced molting), and how the effective altruism community pushed major companies to pledge cage-free eggs. They describe USDA definitions of cage free (verified by inspectors) and free range (a door to outside, with no minimum space or required use), the United Egg Producers certification, and Humane Farm Animal Care's stricter certified humane standards for free range and pasture raised. They also cover broiler chicken growth and welfare, and feed changes. The episode ends with a listener mail about national park versus national forest dispersed camping.

segments.title: Opening banter and chicken software job
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with banter, and Josh recounts his past job at a software company that made tools for commercial chicken operations and his farm visits there. They preview the episode on cage free and free range labels.

segments.title: Effective altruism campaign for cage-free eggs
segments.summary: The hosts describe how a group of effective altruists raised about three million dollars to lobby for legislation and pressure large companies such as Burger King, McDonald's, Whole Foods, and Dollar General to pledge to use only cage-free eggs within a few years.

segments.title: History of egg farming and battery cages
segments.summary: They describe mid-century egg farming with backyard-style hens laying about a hundred eggs a year, then the industrialization of the 1950s that introduced battery cages, with cages stacked and automated manure and egg conveyors. Modern hens lay around three hundred eggs a year due to breeding.

segments.title: Welfare problems of caged hens
segments.summary: The hosts explain that caged hens cannot move, flap wings, or nest, leading to muscle loss and stress. They discuss the need for privacy during laying, Conrad Lorenz's quote on the laying act, hen pecking, and beak trimming.

segments.title: What cage free means under USDA rules
segments.summary: The USDA defines cage free as hens housed so they have unlimited access to food and water and freedom to roam, but it does not specify outdoor access or space. Cage-free barns still hold tens of thousands of hens, with about 10.5 by 11 inches of space per bird. Cage-free standards are verified by inspectors, a key difference from free range.

segments.title: United Egg Producers standards, forced molting, and feed
segments.summary: The hosts describe the United Egg Producers certification and its requirements for natural behaviors, litter, and predator protection. They discuss forced molting through light and feed withholding, and changes in chicken feed away from fish meal toward insect larvae.

segments.title: Broiler chickens and slaughter
segments.summary: The hosts describe broiler chickens bred for breast meat, reaching slaughter weight in about six weeks, with leg problems, ammonia burns in litter, and a dark, crowded barn. Josh recounts a witnessed slaughter on a tour, and they mention a New Yorker account and a YouTube video of automated poultry farming.

segments.title: Free range USDA definition and loophole
segments.summary: The USDA defines free range as continuous access to the outside, with no set size for the opening, no required outdoor time, and no minimum outdoor space. The hosts note that a small hole in a barn could qualify. They cite an Animal Welfare Institute study finding weak substantiation for free range claims. They also explain pasture raised as the more meaningful term, which USDA treats the same as free range.

segments.title: Humane Farm Animal Care standards and buying advice
segments.summary: The hosts describe Humane Farm Animal Care's certified humane standards, including at least six hours of outdoor time and two square feet per bird for free range, and year-round outdoor access with about 108 square feet per bird for pasture raised. They advise listeners to research farms and buy from local farmers markets.

segments.title: Listener mail on national park camping
segments.summary: A listener who is a national park ranger corrects Chuck's claim that dispersed camping is allowed wherever you want in national parks, noting that dispersed camping is more common in national forests, and that national parks often require permits and designated campsites.
